title: Lesson 87: Beyond Agents: Agentic Workflows, Autonomous Pipelines and Self-Healing Systems
description: Applied questions on choosing between an agentic workflow, an autonomous pipeline and a self-healing control loop, on making a failed pipeline resume without losing or duplicating work, and on where a repair loop's permission boundary belongs.

questions.question: What distinguishes an agentic workflow from an autonomous pipeline?
options: The workflow can act without approval, while the pipeline always requires a person to start each run
The workflow fixes the sequence, while the pipeline moves work unattended and survives a crash
The workflow runs on a schedule, while the pipeline is triggered by a person each time
The workflow tolerates crashes, while the pipeline is expected to restart from the beginning
questions.explanation: An agentic workflow runs model and tool calls through a fixed code path, so the sequence is set at design time. An autonomous pipeline moves work between systems unattended, and its own failure is lost or duplicated work rather than a wrong answer.

questions.question: A retry is added to a step that appends a row, and a slow period produces two rows for one case. Which rule did the retry violate?
options: Retries belong on the whole run rather than on an individual tool call
A retry must be bounded by the error budget before it is allowed to run
A retry is safe only when applying it twice equals applying it once
Fresh data is always preferable, so the step should have waited for input
questions.explanation: An idempotent mutation is what makes a retry safe: applying the change twice must equal applying it once. A retry on a plain append produces a duplicate row, so a timeout turns into a data quality incident.

questions.question: A loop proposes to automatically roll back a prompt change after a quality regression. Why should that be a person's decision?
options: Because rollbacks are safe once they are dry-run against recent traffic
Because a rollback should always be paired with a notification to the quality owner
Because the correct repair is to rewrite the affected records rather than the prompt
Because it changes how processed cases should be read, which belongs to a person
questions.explanation: Rolling back a prompt change rewrites the behavior behind cases already processed, which is a data-reinterpretation decision. Anything that changes how already-written data should be interpreted belongs to a person.
